title: Free ChatGPT Users Will Get a Huge Upgrade Next Week
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 7, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            OpenAI is rolling out unlimited text messages for free and Go ChatGPT users next week.
                                            Free users will be able to send as many texts to ChatGPT as they want, though there will be limits on other features and messages.
                                            Plus and Pro users are also getting updates, as OpenAI is rolling out upgrades to its GPT-5.6 Sol model.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        There are 8.3 billion people on this planet, and roughly an eighth of them use ChatGPT. OpenAI confirmed that its infamous AI chatbot now has over one billion weekly active users, a staggering number given that ChatGPT is only three and a half years old. (For reference, that's on par with global Windows users.) Love it or hate it, there's no denying that ChatGPT—and generative AI as a whole—is firmly a part of modern life.  While there are surely many paying ChatGPT customers, the vast majority are using it for free. Though it may be exciting for paid users to try out the company's latest and greatest models, the biggest impact happens whenever OpenAI makes features available free of charge. As it happens, next week, free users are getting perhaps the biggest ChatGPT update in years. Free ChatGPT users are getting unlimited text chats Starting next week, you'll no longer hit a wall when simply texting with ChatGPT. OpenAI says that both free and Go users now have unlimited text chats, which should mean you can send as many text-based messages as you want without running into cooldown periods. Of course, the emphasis here is on "texts." There are absolutely still limits on other ChatGPT features, including messages with files and images, as well as Voice mode and image generation. But for users who primarily use ChatGPT with text-based messages, this update should be more than welcome.  
In addition, OpenAI is switching free and Go users to the company's new GPT-5.6 Luna model, which is designed for "cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads." As such, this model likely won't be as capable as OpenAI's more powerful models available to Pro users, but free users aren't totally left in the lurch: OpenAI says there's a new "Think" button that lets you push Luna further for more complex requests. The experience is much changed from the days when users could jump between different models for free, but perhaps the unlimited text chats will make up for it for most users.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
ChatGPT Pro users are getting some new perks tooOpenAI says that Plus and Pro users are also getting some updates. The company says that its GPT-5.6 Sol model now delivers "more focused" responses, and may issue corrections instead of simply agreeing with the user when they're wrong. It also does away with some of the formatting we've come to expect from AI: Your answer may be more succinct in paragraph form, rather than expansive with bullet points. OpenAI says that Sol makes "fewer mistakes" too, but remember: all AI models hallucinate.     There's also a new slider to push the model from "Instant" to higher effort. The idea is to give users a sliding scale of power, rather than have them switch from distinct models. The more intense you push the model, the longer the responses may take, so OpenAI positions the slider as an option for users to tailor the model to their needs: If you need a quick answer, keep the slider towards the less intense side.

title: Apple Just Blocked Hackers From Taking Advantage of This Serious Security Flaw
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 6, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just released three security updates for macOS that all patch the same serious security vulnerability.
                                            macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 all patch a flaw that can allow hackers to enable Screen Sharing without permission.
                                            It's possible this flaw could let hackers not only see your Mac's screen, but also take over your computer entirely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple released three new security updates for Macs on Thursday, Aug. 6. You don't need to be running the latest version, macOS 26, to take advantage of these updates, either. While the company does have a new Tahoe update, Apple's security updates here include releases for both macOS 15 Sequoia and macOS 14 Sonoma as well—and all of these updates are aimed at patching a flaw that would let hackers share your screen without your permission.Apple's latest macOS security patches fix a  Screen Sharing vulnerability macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 all contain the same, singular security patch: Tracked as CVE-2026-65400, this fix is for a Screen Sharing flaw that Apple says could allow an attacker on your network to "authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials." In layman's terms, this security flaw could let hackers activate Screen Sharing without permission, which would leave the contents of your Mac's display totally open to anyone in the know.Apple's Screen Sharing feature is complex, which is good for usability but potentially dangerous in this case. Not only can people using Screen Sharing see your Mac's display, they can, if prompted, take over your Mac as well. Typically, this requires permissions on both sides to activate, and it's not clear whether that functionality is impacted by this security flaw. But if it is, a bad actor could also theoretically take control of your computer using this flaw—accessing your files, messages, or anything else on your Mac.
The good news is Apple did not say that this flaw was previously publicly disclosed or being actively exploited. As such, chances are good that no hackers out there are currently taking advantage of it. However, that doesn't mean it's an impossibility: Certain AI models, like Claude Mythos, are adept at discovering security vulnerabilities, so hypothetically, someone out there could have found this flaw before Apple did. Luckily, the patch is now out for anyone running the latest three versions of macOS, so all you have to do to protect yourself is update your Mac.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to install this Screen Sharing security patch on Mac  Whether your Mac is brand new or a few versions behind, there's a very good chance you can install one of these security patches. To do so, open System Settings > General > Software Update, let macOS look for the update, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install it.

title: How to Stop Scammers From Showing You Ads on Your Android After Every Phone Call
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're an Android user who is seeing ads pop up after your phone calls, you need not assume this is some new feature you have to learn to live with. It's actually an ad fraud scam, and you can do something about it. Researchers have identified dozens of apps on the Google Play Store that are able to display ads on top of the Android phone interface, a scheme known as AfterCall. How ads are taking over Android callsThis scam originates with seemingly harmless utility apps downloaded from the Google Play Store, such as calendars, alarm clocks, and notepads. When installed, they request overlay permissions, which allow them to appear on top of other apps—and thus display ads over phone calls. These apps can detect when a call ends and will then launch full-screen ads wrapped in a fake call info screen. Since it looks like they are simply part of the call interface, users may be less likely to suspect that they are actually malicious. It's worth noting that overlay permissions can't be granted via a standard pop-up during the app installation process. They are a type of "special permission" that requires users to go into their system settings to enable. Android apps are supposed to request these permissions in context and give a clear reason for doing so. AfterCall scammers are using justifications like alarms not being able to go off or appear correctly without overlay permissions, though some apps will simply crash if users decline permissions.
How to remove AfterCall adsBecause the ads appear out of context—after a phone call and with content unrelated to the utility app—it's harder for users to figure out what's causing them. The utility apps aren't obviously malicious and don't appear on recent app lists when ads are displayed, so it's not obvious that they are connected to the problem. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you are seeing ads pop up after phone calls on your Android, check for apps that have overlay permissions. Go to Settings > Apps > Special app access (this may be hidden behind a three-dot menu) and click on the permission type. Look for apps you don't recognize, or which shouldn't have "display on top" permissions, and uninstall them. You should regularly audit these permissions, and disable any that aren't essential. On the user side, these apps seem to be mostly an annoyance rather than outright malicious programs that are harvesting your sensitive data, though installing any program that requests unnecessary permissions can introduce significant risk. If nothing else, however, these apps do appear to waste brands' advertising dollars and could damage their reputation with users—but you probably just care about how to stop seeing them after your calls.

title: DuckDuckGo Just Made It Easier to Share Links Without Getting Tracked
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 7, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Herstockart via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            DuckDuckGo's new privacy feature on iPhone strips trackers out of URLs before you share them.
                                            You'll need to choose "Copy Clean Link" to take advantage of the feature.
                                            If you simply copy the link as you normally would, you'll copy the trackers as well.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It's tough to stay private on the internet. It's hardly an even playing field: If you use apps and websites as they're designed, your every move is almost guaranteed to be tracked so that companies can compile a profile to target you with ads. That even extends to simple tasks like sharing links with friends: You might think you're simply communicating in private, but as soon as you click "copy" on that link, trackers attach themselves to the URL and come along for the ride.  It doesn't have to be this way. There are many steps you can take to prevent trackers from stalking you across the internet—some more intense than others. And while stripping tracking URLs from links isn't new, it isn't exactly common knowledge, either. That's why whenever a company makes it a bit easier, I'm all for it, so today I'm celebrating DuckDuckGo.DuckDuckGo now makes it easier to strip trackers from links on iPhoneAs highlighted by fellow CNET Group site ZDNet, DuckDuckGo's iOS app now includes a feature that automatically eliminates tracking elements from links. That way, you can share links with friends, family members, and coworkers without worrying about trackers following along. 
The feature, "Copy Clean Link," doesn't do anything you couldn't do yourself. As ZDNet explains, the feature cuts out everything in the URL in question from the "?" on; essentially, all of the tracking information. Without that data, you turn the URL into a "clean" link, so trackers won't necessarily know you're the user who shared that URL in the first place. You can do this yourself by opening the URL and deleting this text manually, but tapping Copy Clean Link is certainly more convenient.Interestingly, the feature doesn't pop up when you select a link the usual way, or even when you hit the Share button. Instead, you'll need to open the link in DuckDuckGo, long-press the address bar, and choose "Copy Clean Link." You'll find the same option if you tap the three lines in the bottom right, then scroll down and choose "Copy Clean Link." If you simply select the URL and use iOS' built-in "Copy" option, you'll grab the full URL—trackers and all.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
DuckDuckGo's Copy Clean Link is an iOS-only feature for nowAt this time, only iPhone users can use "Copy Clean Link" in DuckDuckGo. That doesn't mean that users of other platforms are out of luck: As previously mentioned, you can manually delete all characters in a URL starting with the "?" to achieve the same effect. That's easier done on desktop than mobile, of course.   If you need an alternative, Brave has a "Copy Clean Link" option as well. It works similarly to DuckDuckGo's—you can long-press the address bar on a webpage you're already visiting or, uniquely, you can long-press any link in the browser to get the option too.

title: Apple's iCloud Private Relay Can Actually Expose Your Real IP Address
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 6, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: picture alliance via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            As 404 Media reports, flaws in Apple’s web browser engine allow IP addresses to be revealed when they're supposed to be hidden.
                                            Web requests are made outside of the browser and the protections of Private Relay, meaning that websites that support passkeys can see users' real IP addresses
                                            If you want to keep your IP address hidden and your data encrypted across all apps and browsers on your device, you may want to consider a separate VPN.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you use iCloud Private Relay, Apple's paid IP address masking service, your internet browsing activity may not actually be private. As 404 Media reports, flaws in Apple’s web browser engine allow IP addresses to be revealed, either maliciously or incidentally, even when they're supposed to be hidden. How Private Relay is exposing IP addressesiCloud Private Relay, which is part of Apple's iCloud+ subscription, is supposed to keep both who you are and what sites you visit hidden when you are browsing in Safari. Without it, your network provider and the websites you view can see your IP address and DNS records, which can be used to track your location and browsing history over time. Private Relay is supposed to encrypt DNS records and generate a temporary IP address, keeping any single party, including Apple, from obtaining both. The issue, discovered by security researchers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk, is related to how passkeys work. Web requests are made outside of the browser and the protections of Private Relay, meaning that websites that support passkeys can see users' real IP addresses. Obviously, this impacts Safari traffic, but researchers found the issue in Onion Browser, an iOS app that encrypts traffic through the Tor network. Both 404 Media and TechCrunch verified the issue in their own tests. 
The researchers stated that they informed Apple but haven't been given a timeline for when the vulnerability will be addressed. Apple is generally pretty good on privacy issues, but this isn't the first to arise in recent months. In July, "Hide My Email," the company's email masking service, was revealed to have a vulnerability that actually exposed users' real email addresses. Apple reportedly knew about it for over a year and claimed to have patched it—but it hadn't. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
While Private Relay can be a useful privacy tool—if it works as intended—it's not a true VPN (Virtual Private Network) because it only provides protection when browsing in Safari. If you want to keep your IP address hidden and your data encrypted across all apps and browsers on your device, you may want to consider a separate VPN service.

body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 7, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple updated its trade-in values this week. Some Apple devices are worth more, while some new Android devices were added to the list.
                                            That said, some Android devices actually decreased in value, though only by $5 or $10.
                                            You can apply these trade-in values towards a new purchase or towards Apple's new leasing program.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It's a weird time to be shopping for new tech. On the one hand, "RAMageddon" is making devices more expensive and harder to find; on the other, companies are trying new tactics to get you to buy new stuff more frequently. Take Apple: While it might be more difficult than ever to buy a MacBook Air from the company, Apple will now let you "lease" new products for one-, two-, or three-year agreements. Sure, Macs and iPads might cost more than ever, but you might find it easier to pay those prices over 24 or 36 months, interest-free.Each device's payment plan is presented without a trade-in in mind, but you can apply a trade-in if you choose to lease. Apple will lower your payments based on the value of the device you hand over at the time of signing. The better the value of your device, the lower your payments will be. What's especially interesting given the current tech market is that Apple seems to be sweetening the pot for customers with trade-ins, which will likely only push more towards this "Apple Upgrade" program. Apple increased the trade-in values for many of its products     As reported by 9to5Mac, Apple just increased its trade-in values for a number of products. Most of these are Apple's own devices. The company bumped up the trade-in values of many iPhones, Apple Watches, iPads, and Macs, some more than others. You can now get up to $70 more for your iPhone 16 Pro than you could before, or up to $20 more for your iPhone 13 Pro Max. The actual amount depends on the device in question, and the condition you bring it to Apple in. 
If you're trading in a Mac, the numbers are definitely more significant. Apple bumped some models' trade-in values up over $100, and increased Mac Studio values by $260. That said, other values were much smaller: You can only get another $25 for your iMacs, and Apple didn't change the $315 maximum for your iMac Pro.Here's a full list of Apple's maximum trade-in values, assuming your device meets all qualifications: 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
iPhone trade-in values iPhone 16 Pro Max: Up to $720iPhone 16 Pro: Up to $630iPhone 16 Plus: Up to $485iPhone 16: Up to $480iPhone 16e: Up to $310iPhone 15 Pro Max: Up to $530iPhone 15 Pro: Up to $420iPhone 15 Plus: Up to $340iPhone 15: Up to $335iPhone 14 Pro Max: Up to $405iPhone 14 Pro: Up to $335iPhone 14 Plus: Up to $235iPhone 14: Up to $235iPhone SE (3rd generation): Up to $85iPhone 13 Pro Max: Up to $340iPhone 13 Pro: Up to $285iPhone 13: Up to $205iPhone 13 mini: Up to $155iPhone 12 Pro Max: Up to $240iPhone 12 Pro: Up to $195iPhone 12: Up to $135iPhone 12 mini: Up to $90iPhone SE (2nd generation): Up to $45iPhone 11 Pro Max: Up to $160iPhone 11 Pro: Up to $145iPhone 11: Up to $110iPhone XS Max: Up to $95iPhone XS: Up to $70iPhone XR: Up to $90iPhone X: Up to $60iPhone 8 Plus: Up to $40iPhone 8: Up to $40Apple Watch trade-in valuesApple Watch Series 10: Up to $165Apple Watch Ultra 2: Up to $305Apple Watch Series 9: Up to $135Apple Watch Ultra: Up to $205Apple Watch Series 8: Up to $95Apple Watch SE (2nd generation): Up to $60Apple Watch Series 7: Up to $70Apple Watch Series 6: Up to $45Apple Watch SE (1st generation): Up to $30iPad trade-in valuesiPad Pro: Up to $720iPad: Up to $260iPad Air: Up to $490iPad mini: Up to $300Mac trade-in valuesMacBook Pro: Up to $855MacBook Air: Up to $580iMac: Up to $380iMac Pro: Up to $315Mac mini: Up to $480Mac Studio: Up to $1305Mac Pro: Up to $2195More Android devices qualify for Apple's trade-in program tooEqually noteworthy, however, is that Apple has expanded the list of Android devices eligible for trade-in values too. If you're looking to switch from Android to iPhone, there's a good chance Apple will give you some money towards a new purchase or lease. New this week are the Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G, Google Pixel 9 Pro XL, Google Pixel 9 Pro, Google Pixel 9, OnePlus 13, and OnePlus 13R. While that's good news for these devices owners looking to upgrade, some Android users have some bad news: Apple lowered trade-in values for the following: Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra 5G, Google Pixel 8 Pro, Google Pixel 7 Pro, and Google Pixel 7. Apple only reduced these values by $5 or $10, so it isn't major, but it's interesting to see which devices the company feels aren't worth quite as much. title: You Can Score a MacBook Neo for $599 in the Middle of 'RAMageddon'

        The global memory crisis—commonly referred to as RAMageddon—continues to make just about every piece of tech more expensive. Even Apple, a $4.5 trillion company, can't weather the markets without raising prices. What's more, Apple is struggling to produce enough Macs to meet demand, as you might discover if you try to buy a MacBook Air right now. While it's always a good idea to consider buying used tech, it now makes more sense than ever.As it happens, if you're in the market for Apple's "budget" Mac, the MacBook Neo, it's an excellent time to buy used. Apple originally released the MacBook Neo for $599, a fantastic price for a complete Mac experience. But since the RAM shortage, the company increased its starting price to $699—not bad, but certainly not as enticing an offer as it was at its release just five months ago. The MacBook Neo hits the Apple Refurbished Store But now, the MacBook Neo is officially available directly from Apple at its original $599 price point—as long as you buy it refurbished. But unlike buying a used piece of tech from a friend or a random outlet, Apple's refurbished store isn't unlike buying products new: The company says that it puts "Certified Refurbished" products through a "rigorous" refurbishment process, which includes testing, cleaning, and repackaging. Refurbished Apple products also have the same one-year limited warranty of new products, as well as a 14-day return policy, and you can purchase AppleCare if you so choose. As such, buying a MacBook Neo on the refurbished store should be just about the same experience as buying one new—except for the fact you have an additional $100 in your wallet. You get the same A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM, 13-inch display, 256GB SSD, and two USB ports (one USB 3 and one USB 2). If you want additional storage, as well as an embedded Touch ID sensor, you can upgrade to the 512GB model, also refurbished for $679.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As tech gets more expensive, and companies make fewer products to sell, it makes sense to check out Apple's Refurbished Store for other devices, too. Just about every product category is represented here, to take a look before you buy a device at its full (and inflated) price.

title: How to Protect Yourself From This Massive Ongoing Cryptocurrency Hack
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zooey Liao/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Bad actors have managed to steal more than $130 million in cryptocurrency from offline hardware wallets.
                                            Coldcard wallets had a vulnerability allowing hackers to brute-force users' seed phrases.
                                            Users should update their firmware and migrate to a new seed phrase.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It seems no sooner does someone come up with a method to keep your digital data safe than hackers find a way to subvert it. Today's case in point: Bad actors have stolen more than $130 million in cryptocurrency from users of offline hardware wallets, devices specifically meant to be a safe option for securing bitcoin. Hackers are attacking cold crypto walletsAs TechCrunch reports, multiple groups of hackers have gained access to Coldcard crypto wallets and are continuing to drain funds in an ongoing theft. The wallets, made by Coinkite, are considered "cold," meaning they are not connected to the internet or any other device, and users' keys or seed phrases exist entirely offline. By contrast, "hot" wallets are connected to the internet and include apps and browser extensions. Typically, hot wallets are considered a greater security risk for hacks, theft, malware, and ransomware, but this latest attack exploited a flaw in Coldcard's seed phrase generation process, compromising users' cold wallets. The vulnerability made seeds predictable, so threat actors were able to brute-force victims' passwords—essentially, guess them via trial and error—and gain access to their wallets. 
Hackers carried out more than 200 crypto attacks between January and July of this year, leading to losses of $972 million. That's an increase in the number of events, but a significantly lower amount stolen, compared to the first six months of 2025. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to protect your cryptocurrency wallet According to Coinkite's security advisory, the vulnerability has now been patched for all affected firmware, so users should first install available updates to their devices from the official download pages (linked in the advisory). Users should also migrate their wallets to a new seed phrase following the specific instructions in the advisory. While using a cold wallet should provide greater protection, you may also consider a diversified storage strategy for your cryptocurrency and leave minimal assets in hot wallets at any given time. That way, if one is compromised, it doesn't leave everything vulnerable.

title: Google Maps Has Launched 'Agentic Food Ordering,' but Don't Get Too Excited
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 6, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: S3studio/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google Maps' "Ask Maps" feature can now start an order for you—but you still need to complete it.
                                            The feature is part of a big Ask Maps update Google announced on Thursday, including new options for live transit information.
                                            While it's a taste of an agentic Google Maps, it doesn't really seem to be all that useful, at least based on the description.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        As one of the biggest tech companies in the world, Google is putting its AI features and platforms into each and every one of its products. As such, it’s no surprise that its wildly popular navigation app, Google Maps, is getting the same treatment. While it's easy to use the app without encountering much AI, if you so choose, you can use Google’s latest AI features to find new restaurants, accommodations, or hot spots in your area. And now, Google is boasting that it is launching new "agentic" features that will even allow the app to order food for you—sort of.Ask Maps gets an agentic upgradeBack in March, the company rolled out “Ask Maps,” a chatbot-like interface in Google Maps that taps into Gemini to help you find relevant places on the map. For example, Google says you can “Ask Maps” to find you a restaurant with availability for six at a specific date and time, keeping in mind strict dietary requirements. It’s about what you’d expect from the combination of Gemini and Google Maps: You “chat” with the map to find what you need. Now, Google is expanding on these features, introducing new agentic options to reduce the work you actually have to do to pick up lunch (if not by all that much). Starting today, Google says Ask Maps can handle “complex, multi-step tasks," including functions it can handle on your behalf, and the flagship feature is ordering food for you—or, at least, starting an order.
Ask Maps can't actually order food for youGoogle says you can launch Ask Maps and type something like “order spicy pad kee mao with seafood for me to pick up on my way home." While you might think such a feature would handle the entire request for you, Ask Maps doesn't quite get there. It will, according to Google, look for open restaurants on your route home, and it can even take into consideration your previous orders and dietary needs. But once it floats options, you still need to choose the restaurant you want to order from. Once you do, the agentic features kick in: Google says that Ask Maps will remember your original request and will begin adding the appropriate items to your cart through services like Square and Toast (with Uber Eats support coming soon). However, Ask Maps won't actually order the food for you. You still need to manually review what's been placed in your cart and approve the order before the restaurant will receive it.Other agentic features in Ask MapsAs part of this Ask Maps update, you can also ask about hotels and local events. Google suggests asking the feature something like “For next week’s conference in downtown Miami, find me a decently priced, top-rated hotel with an artsy vibe, within walking distance from a gym and restaurants.” That's certainly a complex request, and, according to Google, Ask Maps will be able to compare prices and availability to find an appropriate hotel. The same goes for things like concerts and comedy shows: Ask Maps will surface results based on your request, but you'll need to click through to actually buy tickets yourself.This isn't yet the agentic future we were promisedI don't have these options on my Google Maps app yet, so I can't personally attest to how well they work, but I'm not sure I'm seeing the vision here. Companies like Google have been promising that agentic features will save us time and rescue us from having to perform tedious or menial tasks. And while this feature does save the 30 seconds or so it takes to building a restaurant order, that's about all it does. Not only do you still have to intervene in multiple aspects of the process (including the actual ordering of the food), it seems like the whole ordeal takes longer than it should. In my view, heading to the restaurant's site, building the order myself, then placing the order (as I'd have to do anyway) is likely more efficient than asking Google's AI to find a restaurant with a specific dish, have it build the order, then have me review it. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Maybe I'll feel differently once I can try it out, and maybe this is just one step into a future where you really can have Google Maps complete a whole order for you. But I'm not sure I'd ever want it to, especially when dealing with ordering multiple items for various people with potential dietary restrictions. Not only would it likely be faster to do it myself, but I'm not sure I'd trust an AI with all those complications. The last thing anyone needs is for an AI to hallucinate and forget to order something with an allergy label. Other new Ask Maps featuresThis update also incorporates Google's "Personal Intelligence," which pulls info from your various Google apps to return more personalized results. As such, you could Ask Maps to find you things to do before your afternoon flight. Google Maps should be able to access Gmail and Google Calendar, where it should find that flight's time and location, in order to fulfill your request with more individualized results than a simple search would. This feature is off by default. There's also a new live data widget for transit instructions, so you can keep tabs on public transit information in real time. You can also suggest Google Maps edits conversationally through Ask Maps, including adding photo attachments.

title: WhatsApp Just Added Five New Group Chat Features, Including '@All'
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Image
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            WhatsApp is rolling out five new features and changes for group chats.
                                            There's now an "@all" function that lets you alert the whole group at once, even if users have the group muted.
                                            There are three new changes to how polls work in group chats on WhatsApp, including the ability to edit polls after posting.
                                            You can also create new group chats from existing groups, for times you need to sidebar with select members of the chat.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        On Tuesday, WhatsApp announced a handful of new features and changes for its app. But unlike the usual feature updates, these changes are specifically for group chats. In total, WhatsApp has five new updates for your groups, one of which will make it much easier to get the entire chat's attention. Here's what's new:  WhatsApp finally gets an "@all" function
    
            
            
                                        Credit: WhatsApp
                    
    
If you've ever used Slack, Google Chat, or any messaging platform with an "@all" function, you know how useful (and potentially disruptive) it can be. By typing "@all" as part of your message, you can force everyone in the group chat to receive a notification for your text. It's especially useful for time-sensitive messages, since it lets you skip tagging all group members one by one. Of course, "@all" can be overused and abused. No one wants unnecessary alerts, but this feature increases the risk that you'll be bothered by someone who didn't think through their "@all" use all that carefully—particularly since the feature breaks through muted group chats. Luckily, there is a notification setting that will let you choose to mute even @all alerts—though keep in mind you'll miss out on these all of those alerts going forward. While @all is available to all group chat members, WhatsApp notes the feature is limited to admins in groups of more than 32 people.   
WhatsApp's group polls now have three new featuresPolls are something I don't use enough in my chat apps. They're a great way to gauge your groups' opinions on any number of topics, from where to go for dinner to which movie you should all see. Now, WhatsApp says it is making polls "even more useful" by adding three new changes to the mix:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You can now set an end time for polls to close, so users have a deadline to respond by. If the poll is particularly sensitive, you can hide responders' names, so people can vote more freely.Finally, you can edit poll questions within 15 minutes of posting, in case you made a mistake or need to make a question clearer.  You can create new WhatsApp group chats from existing groups
    
            
            
                                        Credit: WhatsApp
                    
    
The next time you need to create a smaller group chat featuring members of an existing group, you no longer need to build it from scratch. Instead, you can make new group chats from your current groups, which should make splitting off much easier. WhatsApp sees this as a great way to "plan a surprise party" or "coordinate event logistics," but we all know this is going to be used in, let's say, less kind ways. Yes, the ability to create a side chat from a main chat will be used to talk smack inconspicuously. (I imagine the first text in these breakout group chats will be "Oh my god, can you believe they just said that?")

            ExperienceJoel Cunningham is Lifehacker’s Deputy Editor. He has 15 years of experience as a writer and editor. Previously, he was managing editor of content marketing for Barnes & Noble, where he founded the Barnes & Noble Sci-Fi & Fantasy Blog.

            Credit: Lifehacker / Xteink
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The tech world is usually all about selling you the bigger, better, newer model every year, so I still find it funny that the most talked-about e-reader of 2026 isn't a flashy new Kindle or a pricey Boox tablet, but a tiny, cheap e-ink device from an upstart Chinese tech company. Xteink makes e-readers small enough to fit in your pocket—any pocket—an irresistible form factor that has garnered them a devoted online following despite their slightly janky software.The Xteink X4 was my own personal tech upgrade of the year for 2025, and this year's smaller X3 and more fully-featured X4 Pro are even better. Every time I'm using one of them in public, I get asked what it is and where I got it, and I can't stop recommending them to people looking to find more ways to reduce their doomscrolling and read more books. If that's you, it's the time to buy, because today only Xteink is offering 15% off on both the X4 and the X3—and the latter was already marked down 13%, so the additional discount takes it to its lowest price ever.
Given the discount takes both devices down to the same sub-$60 price, if you're not sure which one to buy, there's really only one factor to consider: The Xteink X4 is pretty small—with a 4.3-inch screen, it's roughly the size of a small wallet—while the 3.7-inch X3 is even smaller, roughly the size of a credit card. Otherwise, the devices are fairly similar, the biggest differences being slightly better resolution on the X3 (thanks solely to the smaller screen increasing the number of pixels per inch) and different charging cables (in order to maximize space, the X3 charges with an included pogo pin adapter, while the X4 uses USB-C). 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Personally, I like the X3 better, as the smaller screen is still comfortable to read on, and it's so small I often forget I'm carrying it—until I need to pull it out to read while I wait for the subway, so I can avoid looking at my phone.

title: Here's When ChatGPT Atlas Will Shut Down for Good
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 5, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Philip Dulian/picture alliance via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            OpenAI is ending support for ChatGPT Atlas, its dedicated AI browser, after just 10 months.
                                            The company encourages users to move to the ChatGPT desktop app, which includes agentic browsing features.
                                            If you're looking for a dedicated AI browser, there are other options out there.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        "Agentic" is the tech buzzword of the moment. The phrase describes an AI tool you can ask to perform tasks automatically on your behalf. Maybe the bot will order your favorite dish on DoorDash, or call a car for you without you needing to open the Uber app. Perhaps in a few years, AI assistants will be scheduling your meetings, or screening interviewees for a job based on your direction—though I'm not sure we've cracked the simple tasks just yet. Regardless, most companies that make AI technologies are pushing these agents in some way, shape, or form—including into their AI-powered browsers. Companies like Perplexity have browsers that offer agentic features that invite you to task your AI with performing tasks on the web. Rather than shop on Amazon yourself, perhaps you can ask an AI assistant to do it. Instead of painstakingly compiling sources for a paper, maybe your bot will find them for you. That's the gist, anyway.However, despite the focus on agentic AI, one of the biggest AI companies in the world is shuttering its own AI browser. OpenAI has announced it will soon discontinue ChatGPT Atlas, a venture it only launched last October. The shutdown comes just months after the company also shut down Sora, its AI-generated short-form video platform, marking the second high-profile OpenAI product of 2026 to go under.  
OpenAI will officially shut down ChatGPT Atlas on Sunday, Aug. 9. While it won't delete the browser from your devices, it may stop working as intended. OpenAI says that after this date, ChatGPT Atlas may not open, browse, or support "browser-based agentic workflows." As such, the company encourages users to export or save all of their ChatGPT Atlas data, including bookmarks and pages.       In addition, ChatGPT Atlas won't receive security updates going forward. That makes it especially important to stop using it after Aug. 9: While all browsers and devices that connect to the internet should be running the latest security patches as soon as they're available, AI browsers are particularly vulnerable. Because they have agentic features, hackers can take advantage of the automated AI to trick it into performing tasks on their behalf instead of yours. A bot can't tell the difference between your commands and a malicious prompt hidden on a website it browses. These browsers are already a security risk—ChatGPT Atlas itself had a major vulnerability at launch—but using an AI browser that is no longer supported is beyond dangerous.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What other AI browsers are there to choose from?If you ask OpenAI, you don't have to leave its sandbox in order to play with AI browsing features. The company is pointing users to its ChatGPT desktop app, which includes some browsing features, like multiple tabs, downloads, account login support, and "improved navigation." To me, those sound like perks for active ChatGPT users, but not a replacement for a dedicated browser. That said, there is a feature called "Computer Use" that lets ChatGPT take over certain apps on your Mac, including your browser.   However, if you're looking for a true ChatGPT Atlas replacement, you have options, the most notable of which is probably Perplexity Comet, one of the first agentic browsers on the market. Opera also makes its own AI browser, called Neon, if you're already a fan of that company's offerings. If you used Arc before it went belly-up a few years back, you might be happy to learn the company now develops an AI browser called Dia. Any of these will be a more full-featured replacement for ChatGPT Atlas than settling for the ChatGPT app.
